  reference-only, and the dataclass field renamed `severe_cost_range_usd` so no
  reader mistakes them for the typical case again.
- Checkers updated rather than left certifying stale text: the arithmetic pass is
  now **89 checks** and reports both findings **closed and checked**, not merely
  recorded. The decision paper's **65 checks** still reproduce (it documents the
  withdrawn figures, which is its job).

**Two things a future reader will otherwise trip over.** First, A2 §3.2 says 1.77x
at 500 axles and D08 §5 says 2.01x — different questions on the same inputs (A2
charges the pilot with no benefit; D08 credits the 200-axle pilot with its actual
benefit). A2 §3.2 now states that difference explicitly. Second, **D08 §2 scopes the
pilot at 100–200 axles**, so any pilot-year benefit computed at 500 was contradicting
the document's own scope. That defect was mine, introduced in the first restatement
and caught before commit.

## Ledger replication series — built 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

`backend/ledger_replication.py` executes the cadence D09 §4.5.4 already
specified: monthly full, weekly incremental, every bundle chained to the
previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten.
`inspect` opens every bundle, recomputes its digest, verifies it against the
predecessor, and reports a missing period. 32 tests; full suite **112**.

**It deliberately does not transmit.** D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no
outbound network, so the series accumulates in `--series-dir` on the box and
carrying it to backup media is the Railroad's step under §3.3. The owner chose
this over a network push on 2026-11-10; the reasoning is in
`assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**Two audits found nine material defects before this was called built** — the
count is in the assets file rather than here, but the shape is worth carrying:
the release verifier rejected every full export, `inspect` could not see
tampering or gaps, the period walker hung on a 53-week ISO year, concurrent runs
duplicated bundles, and one test passed only because the check it guarded was
absent. A green suite of 108 preceded all of it.

## Export hardened at chat-4's validation pass, 2026-11-10

Found by attacking the artifact rather than re-reading it, when the owner asked
for the completed work to be validated: **a written bundle accepted any extra
top-level field and both verifiers still returned `ok=True`.** The signature
covers a selected tuple and the digest names its fields, so a key added beside
them was unsigned — changeable after signing, and readable by a recipient as
though the bundle attested it.

Both `backend/ledger_export.py` and `tools/verify_ledger_export.py` now reject a
bundle whose top level is not exactly `format` / `manifest` / `records` /
`signature`, with the check named `bundle_no_extras`. The signing construction is
unchanged: a named field list is the correct way to sign, because it puts the
covered set in code rather than in the document. The gap was the absence of a
check on what else the document contains. One test added and mutation-tested in
both files; suite 113 → **114**.

## Status at close — every completed task re-verified against the repository

Not re-read. Executed: the suite (114/0), the arithmetic pass (97/97), the
decision paper (65/65); the withdrawn 2.0×/4.1× pair confirmed absent as a live
claim in both documents; `roi.py` constants read back from the module ($999,750
expected cost, 4.8/1.5 h MTTD); the replication module built a real series and
`inspect` verified it, then **detected** both a manifest edit and the extra-field
case; the rebuilt workbook reopened and its cached values checked ($370,000
pilot, ROI 2.0653).

**The workbook swap was completed on 2026-11-10 after Excel released its lock.**
`AxiomDynamics-ROI-Calculator.xlsx` in the docket is now the corrected file —
$370,000 pilot year, three-year ROI 2.0653×, agreeing with A2 §5.1. The
intermediate `…rebuilt.xlsx` and `REPLACE-WORKBOOK.bat` were deleted once the
swap was confirmed byte-identical, because a second copy of the same workbook
under a different name is how the staleness got missed in the first place.

## Transcript — chat-4 extracted and committed at close, 2026-11-10

The standing rule is that a phase is not finished until its assets and its
conversation are in this repository. Chat-4's raw log was extracted at close:
5,667 events, 12 MB, into
`project-logs/transcripts/raw/2026-11-10-chat-4-snapshot.jsonl`, with the
readable extract at `project-logs/transcripts/2026-11-10-chat-4.md` — 704 turns
of which **six are the owner's**.

**A defect in the extractor was fixed in this pass.** `extract_transcript.py`
wrote a hard-coded `"# Chat-3"` heading into every extract regardless of which
session it was processing, so chat-4's file opened under the wrong title. It now
derives the heading from the output filename (`…-chat-4.md` → `# Chat-4`) and
falls back to the filename stem otherwise.

**Build history regenerated at 39 pages (chat-6).** Stage 10 was added for
chat-6 — authenticated disposition entry and the inert guard the audit found —
and Part VII's two entry-gating rows were rewritten rather than left to contradict
the code. The paragraph below records the chat-5 revision. Stage 9 was added for
chat-5 — the ledger audit, the ingest path, the supply-chain tools and
attribution — and Part VII's gap register was rebuilt rather than patched: the
ingest row, the attribution row and the supply-chain rows all described states
that chat-5 changed, and three of them had drifted into claiming more than the
code did. The earlier revision, at chat-4's close, is recorded above: Part VII
still described Findings 1 and 2 as open, which had been true when written in
chat-3; both are now closed with their resolution kept rather than deleted. Stage 8 was extended to carry the model
decision, and the status-at-a-glance table was corrected — its test count, its
replication row and its commercial-numbers row were all stale.

## Signed ledger export — built 2026-11-10 (AD-3 part two), commit `d9c83d4`

`backend/ledger_export.py` builds an HMAC-SHA256-signed bundle: manifest (id
range, record count, head hash, the ledger's own head, covered-field list,
canonicalisation rule, chain status, previous bundle digest), every record in
canonical form, and a signature over the whole. `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`
verifies it **without importing anything from `backend/`**, from an empty
directory, with `-I` — the recipient needs the bundle, the key, and a Python
standard library, nothing else.

**Why HMAC and not Ed25519:** the stdlib has no asymmetric primitive, and
hand-rolling one in a product that tells CISOs it does not hand-roll crypto
would be worse than the gap. The two limits — cannot name the signer, cannot
date itself — are stated in B01 §4.5a rather than footnoted.

**The audit caught a serious hole, and this is the part worth remembering.**
The first version let a total wipe verify green: delete every row, export
honestly, and a recipient holding the previous bundle was told everything
passed. Each check was individually correct; none compared the bundle against
one already held. Fixed by recording the ledger's own head in every bundle and
failing when a later bundle reports a shorter ledger (`no_truncation`), plus
`genesis_anchor` for rows deleted from the front. Export tests are now 43; the
suite at the time of that build was 80. Three tests assert a failure to detect on purpose, recording disclosed
limits rather than hiding them.

**What it does not do:** detect a ledger wiped before the first bundle in a
series; replicate off-box on a schedule; name the signer. D09 §4.5 makes bundle
retention and a written key-custody procedure the controls that carry that
weight.

Internal account: `assets/ledger-export-build-2026-11-09.md`.

## Transcript — re-snapshotted and committed 2026-11-10, commit `53ad93a`

The standing rule is that a phase is not finished until its assets and its
conversation are in this repository. The chat-3 raw log was re-snapshotted at
close (5,032 events, 17.1 MB) into
`project-logs/transcripts/raw/2026-11-10-chat-3-snapshot.jsonl`, and the
readable extract rebuilt from it — 641 turns, of which **ten are the owner's**;
everything else is assistant text and tool calls.

The mid-session snapshot was deleted rather than kept: it was byte-for-byte a
prefix of the new one, so keeping it would have added 13 MB and no information.
The extractor now lives in the repo at `project-logs/extract_transcript.py`
instead of a shell heredoc, with the rules and the trap that cost a cycle on the
first attempt written into it — the role is the top-level `type` field, not
`message["role"]`.

## Append-only disposition ledger — built 2026-11-09 (AD-3)

The gap that had been disclosed in six documents since `cf2e6ba` is closed at
the code level.

- `backend/store.py` rewritten. Records are inserted, never updated. A second
  decision on an advisory is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`; the earlier row
  keeps its content and timestamp. `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` triggers
  `RAISE(ABORT)`, so the guarantee lives in the schema rather than in convention.
  Every row stores `prev_hash` and `record_hash` — a SHA-256 over its own
  canonical content plus the predecessor's hash — and `verify_chain()`
  recomputes the whole chain and names the first row that fails.
- Migration from the v1 one-row-per-advisory table runs inside `init_db()`,
  preserves the surviving decision and its original timestamp, and does not
  fabricate history that the old schema had already destroyed.
- 17 adversarial tests in `tests/test_store.py`: an UPDATE, a DELETE, a second
  disposition, a tampered row, a removed row, and two migration shapes. Each
  asserts the attempt fails or is detected. `tests/run_tests.py` now discovers
  every `test_*.py`, so the total suite is 38.
- New routes: `GET /api/warrant/{id}/disposition` (full trail, with `chain_ok`)
  and `GET /api/ledger/verify`. The dashboard shows the decision trail under the
  form and marks a corrected decision as superseding an earlier record.

**What it does not prove, and the docket now says so in these words:** the chain
is tamper-*evident*, not tamper-*proof*. A party with write access to the
database file can drop the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash. That
is why items 6 and 8 above stay open.

Docket corrected in the same commit: B01 §4 and §7 items 2/8, D09 §4.4 and the
audit-logging row, F09 Part 6 and Part 7, F00, B02, C02, D12, D14 §5, D00 Part V
and Part VI, and the root README.

## A1 builder — fixed in chat-3

Two defects in `A1-ROI-MODEL/build_roi_calculator.py`, both cosmetic to the
workbook but both real if anyone runs it:

- The sheet-5 assumptions note attributed a **2% catastrophic escalation rate** to
  a model whose cell B17 has held **0.05%** since the correction. A reader
  reconciling the sheet against its own footnote would find a ten-fold conflict.
- The script saved to `/sessions/.../mnt/outputs/...`, a path inside the destroyed
  chat-1 sandbox, so running it raised `FileNotFoundError`. It now writes beside
  itself.


## Git state

The sandbox **cannot reach GitHub** — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with
HTTP 403 from the proxy. Its `origin/main` ref therefore only advances when the
owner pushes and the sandbox is told the result. Do not trust it as evidence of
remote state without checking the commits page.

**Pushing is done by the owner**, with `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. It
prints the commits waiting to go up and verifies afterwards.

**Last confirmed pushed state, 2026-11-10:** the owner's push moved the remote to
`bb99cdd`. Everything after it is local and waiting, and every edit to this file
adds to the queue — so the count is deliberately not written here. Run
`git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.

**The host repo at `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` is authoritative for push state.**
Verify by opening the commits page.

**The line-ending trap.** `git status` in this repo lists nearly every tracked file
as modified on a fresh Windows checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against
LF blobs, not a content change — `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty.
There is no `.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset. **Always check with
`--ignore-cr-at-eol` before believing a diff stat**, and never let an editor
rewrite a whole file's endings into a commit: doing so once during chat-3 turned a
two-line fix into 1,248 changed lines, which had to be reset and recommitted.


## What was lost in the chat-1 → chat-2 transition

Recorded here so nobody goes looking for it:

- Three commits built at the end of chat-1 (`0b66d21`, `cb4f74d`, and the
  F00/D07/Q6 work) existed only in the old sandbox. **`F00` Rule 7, the D07 §14
  rewrite and Q6 were rebuilt into the repository in chat-2.** The project-logs
  structure was rebuilt. The transcripts were not and cannot be — see
  `README.md`.
- Because the rebuild is a reconstruction rather than a recovery, the wording may
  differ from what chat-1 wrote. The *decisions* are identical; the prose is not
  guaranteed to be. Do not treat the current text as a restoration of an earlier
  draft.

## Standing instructions

- **[WORK LOCATION] All project work is written directly into this repository, first pass, and committed in the same pass.** No drafts in sandbox scratch space — that is how chat-1's final phase was lost.
- Keep the same concept throughout — consistency of framing across every document.
- Internal analysis goes in `assets/`, never `client-assets/`.
- Verify against the file before writing the claim.

## Why chat-1's work was lost — the mechanism

Not a deletion. The work was never on the owner's machine.

Chat-1 built the repo inside a temporary sandbox container. To get anything out
it bundled the repo, embedded the bundle in a `.bat`, and the owner ran it once —
which is how `de9b245` reached GitHub. **Everything chat-1 did after that push
stayed in the container**, including the F00 Rule 7 work, the D07 §14 rewrite, Q6
and the transcripts. The bundle was never remade. When the session ended the
container was destroyed and took all of it.

The failure was treating "committed" as "safe." Inside that container it only
meant "saved somewhere that is about to be emptied."

**The rule that follows:** there is no automatic export. A commit in the sandbox
is not durable until it is in `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` and pushed. Never tell
the owner work is saved without saying where it physically is.

130	## 6. Scale envelope
131	
132	Per edge box, designed for: one to six detector feeds, up to ~5,000 monitored axles, sub-second inference per unit, disposition volume in the low hundreds per day. Beyond that, additional boxes — which is exactly what the per-site platform fee in D08/A2 prices.
133	
134	## 7. Production decisions required — where the code differs today
135	
136	**This section is the honest gap list. It must be emptied before any contract cites B01.**
137	
138	| # | Item | Current state | Required for production |
139	|---|---|---|---|
140	| 1 | Reviewer authentication | **Partly built 2026-11-11.** `backend/attribution.py` implements the certification registry: per-reviewer 32-byte keys, an append-only hash-chained registry with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`BEFORE INSERT … OR REPLACE` triggers, and HMAC attestations over each row's `record_hash` that travel inside exported records. `attest()` refuses an unregistered key, a revoked key, a key registered to a different reviewer, and a key registered under a different certificate; `register()` refuses a key revoked anywhere in its history, **and — since 2026-11-11 — a live key presented under a second reviewer**, which it previously accepted, silently transferring the key and locking its original holder out of attesting. A renewed certificate for the same reviewer may still reuse the key. Both verifiers check reviewer, certificate, registration-before-attestation and revocation-on-time, and recompute the attestation when the reviewer's key is supplied **together with the name bound to it** — a key alone cannot establish the label, because the HMAC covers the row hash and not the name. The registry is **hash-chained, not signed**: it is tamper-evident to a reader who recomputes the chain, which is weaker than authentication and is described that way everywhere it appears. **Entry is now gated 2026-11-11.** `backend/accounts.py` binds an account to a live certification record already in the registry, stores a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 verifier (600,000 iterations, per-account salt) rather than a passphrase, and issues a bearer token of which only the SHA-256 digest is stored. `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` requires that token: reviewer name and certificate ID are taken from the resolved session and **never from the request body**, and a body carrying either field is refused rather than ignored. `resolve_session` re-checks that the session is unrevoked and unexpired, that the account is live, **and that the certification behind it is still live**, so a certificate revoked mid-session stops writing immediately; a second check runs inside the ledger's own write transaction, closing the resolve-to-INSERT window. With no account enrolled the path is **closed**, not opened back up to free text. The account register is append-only and hash-chained over salt, iteration count and verifier — a swap of any of the three would hand over the account. **Established by an independent audit told to falsify it**, which found the transaction guard inert because it returned a boolean and the caller discarded it; fixed, with the exploit reproduced verbatim against the fix's removal. What this still does not do is prove a human was at the keyboard, protect the token in transit (§7 item 10), or make attestation stronger — and entry now requires an attestation as well as a live session (2026-11-11): the caller must present a registered reviewer key, it is checked against the session's reviewer and certificate, and the attestation is written inside the ledger's own transaction so a refused key leaves no row | AD-2 remainder: **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure** — a written process, **now written in D09 §8.4**, with issuance in `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py`. **The signed key directory is built 2026-11-11:** `backend/key_directory.py` publishes a signed list of reviewer↔key_id↔cert_id bindings (no key material), `tools/publish_key_directory.py` builds it on the Platform host and refuses if the registry chain does not verify, and `tools/verify_key_directory.py` verifies it on a recipient machine importing nothing from `backend/`. It **proves the export-key holder authored those bindings, not that they are entitled to** — the signature is symmetric — so it is portable and tamper-evident rather than authenticated. Attestation is required at entry since 2026-11-11 |
141	| 2 | Ledger append-only | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-11.** Insert-only write path; `supersedes_id` for corrections; `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE` triggers abort, plus `BEFORE INSERT ... WHEN EXISTS` refusing `INSERT OR REPLACE` over an existing id; SHA-256 chain across rows | Built — superseded decisions retained, chain verified on demand |
142	| 3 | Timestamps | SQLite `datetime('now')` default | Server-generated with NTP-synced clock |
143	| 4 | Storage durability | The demonstration environment's storage is ephemeral — the demo database is lost on spin-down | Persistent volume on Railroad hardware |
144	| 5 | Sensor ingest | **The validation chain and collector authentication are built 2026-11-11; the payload schema is not the Railroad's.** `backend/ingest.py` implements B02 §2's three gates (schema → timestamp → plausibility) over a versioned demonstration schema, fails closed, and logs every outcome. **Ingest is now authenticated 2026-11-11.** `backend/ingest_auth.py` gives a collector its own credential, deliberately separate from a reviewer account: a collector is enrolled by name, receives a 32-byte bearer token once (only the SHA-256 digest is stored), and the registry is append-only and hash-chained. `POST /api/ingest` checks the credential **before reading or logging the body** — an earlier draft logged unparseable bodies on the way in, so any anonymous caller could append rows to the ingest log; the gate now runs first, and a missing, dead or unissued token is a 401 while a deployment with no enrolled collector is **closed (503)** rather than reopened to anonymous traffic. A collector token has **no TTL and is not invalidated by revoking its enrollment**, because a collector is scheduled software rather than a person who has left; revoking stops new tokens being issued. **A Railroad payload is accepted, validated and logged — but the demonstration fleet still generates its signals from physics equations on synthetic traces, so no number in the demo moves because of ingested data.** | Real detector payload schema, defined and versioned with the Railroad |
145	| 6 | Time source | Host clock, unsynchronized | NTP to Railroad-approved source |
146	| 7 | Update mechanism | **Partly addressed 2026-11-11.** Deploys are still via git, but a release can now be built reproducibly and signed: `tools/sign_release.py` writes a deterministic archive plus the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 expects, signs it with a detached GPG signature, and verifies against a supplied public key. The release path installs with `--require-hashes`. **What is missing is organisational, not code:** a GPG key must be generated, its custody written, its public half published by a route the Railroad trusts, and `requirements.txt` pinned on a host with index access (`tools/pin_requirements.py`) — until that last step the Docker build **fails by design** rather than installing unpinned | Offline signed update packages with a published key, see D06 and D09 §7.3 |
147	| 8 | Audit export | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-11.** Signed HMAC-SHA256 bundle written by `backend/ledger_export.py`; verified by `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`, which imports nothing from the Platform. Bundles chain via `previous_export_hash` and carry the ledger head so truncation is detectable against a held bundle. Verification requires the bundle to be exactly the four signed parts — an added top-level field is rejected with `bundle_no_extras`, and duplicate JSON keys are refused outright. **2026-11-11: `history_continues` now catches a rewritten history against a held bundle, which `no_truncation` alone did not.** 48 adversarial tests | Built — but see the trust-anchor item below, and read §4.5a on the one-record scope of `history_continues` |
148	| 9 | Repo hygiene | `axiom.db` and `__pycache__` were committed | Corrected; `.gitignore` added |
149	| 10 | TLS on the box | Plain HTTP | TLS or network isolation; Railroad's internal standard |
150	| 11 | **Export signing key provenance** | The key is an operator-held 32-byte secret with a printed `key_id`; its authenticity rests on a written custody procedure, not on a signature from a trusted issuer. The signature is symmetric, so any verifier can also forge | AD-2: bind the key to an issued certification record, or replace HMAC with an asymmetric signature and a published public key |
151	| 12 | **Off-box replication** | **Partly closed 2026-11-10.** `backend/ledger_replication.py` now produces the D09 §4.5.4 series on a cadence — monthly full, weekly incremental, each bundle chained to the previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten — and its `inspect` verifies each bundle against the one before it and flags a missing period. What it does **not** do is move anything off the box, deliberately: D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no outbound network, so carrying the series away is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3. Until that step happens a lost disk still loses the ledger, and a missed run is *visible* in the series rather than prevented by it | Scheduled export to a second host, with the receipt acknowledged per D09 §4.4 |
152	
153	Items 1 and 5 are **blocking** — the certification and detection claims cannot be made until they close. **Item 5's endpoint authentication closed 2026-11-11,** leaving the real payload schema as its only open part. **Item 1's entry half closed 2026-11-11:** a disposition now requires a live session token, and the reviewer identity on the row comes from that session rather than from the request. What keeps the item open is not the software's behaviour but the human process behind a credential — key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — which no amount of code settles; that process is now **written** (D09 §8.4) and is therefore auditable under §10.1, but writing it does not put a named person at the keyboard. The signed key directory is now built, and the item's last column records what it does and does not prove. Authenticating a credential holder is not authenticating a person, and this document does not claim it is. Items 3, 4, 6, 7, 11 and 12 are required before a production licence, not before a demo. Items 2, 8 and 9 are built. Item 10 is specific to the demonstration host and does not arise where the Platform runs on the Railroad's isolated network.
154	
155	**Items 2 and 8, closed and what that changes.** The append-only guarantee is enforced by the database rather than by convention, and the export is signed and independently verifiable. Two suites test the two halves adversarially: 17 tests attempt an `UPDATE`, a `DELETE`, a second disposition, a tampered row and a removed row against the ledger, and 43 tests attempt to truncate, erase, extend, re-sign, reorder, re-key, wholly rewrite a bundle, and smuggle an unsigned field into one. A third suite of 58 tests attacks the attribution path: an attestation lifted onto another row, an attestation made under an unregistered, revoked, mismatched-reviewer or mismatched-certificate key, a registration date shifted, a registry entry edited or replaced, a manifest that miscounts what it carries, and a parity check that both verifiers catch the same seven structural tampers after the bundle is re-signed. **That suite was then handed to a separate agent whose instruction was to falsify the claim rather than review the code**, and it found a defect the whole suite had missed: the `reviewer` label in an exported attestation was not covered by the HMAC at all, so a holder of any registered reviewer key could relabel another reviewer's row and both verifiers returned a pass. It is fixed — the verifier must now be told which reviewer a key belongs to — and the reason it existed is §4.5a. **The erasure tests exist because the first version of this export passed a total wipe** — every row deleted, an honest empty bundle, a clean verification — and only an independent audit caught it. What remains open has moved from *"there is no signature"* to *"the signature cannot name the export signer, cannot date itself, and cannot detect a first-export-after-wipe"* — item 11, item 12 and the custody procedure. **Per-disposition attribution no longer belongs on that list**: a bundle can now say which registered reviewer attested a row.
156	
157	## 8. Costs of the architectural choices
158	
159	Stated plainly, because the Railroad's IT team will find them anyway and it is better that we said it first.

**This section is the honest gap list. It must be emptied before any contract cites B01.**

| # | Item | Current state | Required for production |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reviewer authentication | **Partly built 2026-11-11.** `backend/attribution.py` implements the certification registry: per-reviewer 32-byte keys, an append-only hash-chained registry with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`BEFORE INSERT … OR REPLACE` triggers, and HMAC attestations over each row's `record_hash` that travel inside exported records. `attest()` refuses an unregistered key, a revoked key, a key registered to a different reviewer, and a key registered under a different certificate; `register()` refuses a key revoked anywhere in its history, **and — since 2026-11-11 — a live key presented under a second reviewer**, which it previously accepted, silently transferring the key and locking its original holder out of attesting. A renewed certificate for the same reviewer may still reuse the key. Both verifiers check reviewer, certificate, registration-before-attestation and revocation-on-time, and recompute the attestation when the reviewer's key is supplied **together with the name bound to it** — a key alone cannot establish the label, because the HMAC covers the row hash and not the name. The registry is **hash-chained, not signed**: it is tamper-evident to a reader who recomputes the chain, which is weaker than authentication and is described that way everywhere it appears. **Entry is now gated 2026-11-11.** `backend/accounts.py` binds an account to a live certification record already in the registry, stores a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 verifier (600,000 iterations, per-account salt) rather than a passphrase, and issues a bearer token of which only the SHA-256 digest is stored. `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` requires that token: reviewer name and certificate ID are taken from the resolved session and **never from the request body**, and a body carrying either field is refused rather than ignored. `resolve_session` re-checks that the session is unrevoked and unexpired, that the account is live, **and that the certification behind it is still live**, so a certificate revoked mid-session stops writing immediately; a second check runs inside the ledger's own write transaction, closing the resolve-to-INSERT window. With no account enrolled the path is **closed**, not opened back up to free text. The account register is append-only and hash-chained over salt, iteration count and verifier — a swap of any of the three would hand over the account. **Established by an independent audit told to falsify it**, which found the transaction guard inert because it returned a boolean and the caller discarded it; fixed, with the exploit reproduced verbatim against the fix's removal. What this still does not do is prove a human was at the keyboard, protect the token in transit (§7 item 10), or make attestation stronger — and entry now requires an attestation as well as a live session (2026-11-11): the caller must present a registered reviewer key, it is checked against the session's reviewer and certificate, and the attestation is written inside the ledger's own transaction so a refused key leaves no row | AD-2 remainder: **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure** — a written process, **now written in D09 §8.4**, with issuance in `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py`. **The signed key directory is built 2026-11-11:** `backend/key_directory.py` publishes a signed list of reviewer↔key_id↔cert_id bindings (no key material), `tools/publish_key_directory.py` builds it on the Platform host and refuses if the registry chain does not verify, and `tools/verify_key_directory.py` verifies it on a recipient machine importing nothing from `backend/`. It **proves the export-key holder authored those bindings, not that they are entitled to** — the signature is symmetric — so it is portable and tamper-evident rather than authenticated. Attestation is required at entry since 2026-11-11 |
| 2 | Ledger append-only | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-11.** Insert-only write path; `supersedes_id` for corrections; `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE` triggers abort, plus `BEFORE INSERT ... WHEN EXISTS` refusing `INSERT OR REPLACE` over an existing id; SHA-256 chain across rows | Built — superseded decisions retained, chain verified on demand |
| 3 | Timestamps | SQLite `datetime('now')` default | Server-generated with NTP-synced clock |
| 4 | Storage durability | The demonstration environment's storage is ephemeral — the demo database is lost on spin-down | Persistent volume on Railroad hardware |
| 5 | Sensor ingest | **The validation chain and collector authentication are built 2026-11-11; the payload schema is not the Railroad's.** `backend/ingest.py` implements B02 §2's three gates (schema → timestamp → plausibility) over a versioned demonstration schema, fails closed, and logs every outcome. **Ingest is now authenticated 2026-11-11.** `backend/ingest_auth.py` gives a collector its own credential, deliberately separate from a reviewer account: a collector is enrolled by name, receives a 32-byte bearer token once (only the SHA-256 digest is stored), and the registry is append-only and hash-chained. `POST /api/ingest` checks the credential **before reading or logging the body** — an earlier draft logged unparseable bodies on the way in, so any anonymous caller could append rows to the ingest log; the gate now runs first, and a missing, dead or unissued token is a 401 while a deployment with no enrolled collector is **closed (503)** rather than reopened to anonymous traffic. A collector token has **no TTL and is not invalidated by revoking its enrollment**, because a collector is scheduled software rather than a person who has left; revoking stops new tokens being issued. **A Railroad payload is accepted, validated and logged — but the demonstration fleet still generates its signals from physics equations on synthetic traces, so no number in the demo moves because of ingested data.** | Real detector payload schema, defined and versioned with the Railroad |
| 6 | Time source | Host clock, unsynchronized | NTP to Railroad-approved source |
| 7 | Update mechanism | **Partly addressed 2026-11-11.** Deploys are still via git, but a release can now be built reproducibly and signed: `tools/sign_release.py` writes a deterministic archive plus the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 expects, signs it with a detached GPG signature, and verifies against a supplied public key. The release path installs with `--require-hashes`. **What is missing is organisational, not code:** a GPG key must be generated, its custody written, its public half published by a route the Railroad trusts, and `requirements.txt` pinned on a host with index access (`tools/pin_requirements.py`) — until that last step the Docker build **fails by design** rather than installing unpinned | Offline signed update packages with a published key, see D06 and D09 §7.3 |
| 8 | Audit export | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-11.** Signed HMAC-SHA256 bundle written by `backend/ledger_export.py`; verified by `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`, which imports nothing from the Platform. Bundles chain via `previous_export_hash` and carry the ledger head so truncation is detectable against a held bundle. Verification requires the bundle to be exactly the four signed parts — an added top-level field is rejected with `bundle_no_extras`, and duplicate JSON keys are refused outright. **2026-11-11: `history_continues` now catches a rewritten history against a held bundle, which `no_truncation` alone did not.** 48 adversarial tests | Built — but see the trust-anchor item below, and read §4.5a on the one-record scope of `history_continues` |
| 9 | Repo hygiene | `axiom.db` and `__pycache__` were committed | Corrected; `.gitignore` added |
| 10 | TLS on the box | Plain HTTP | TLS or network isolation; Railroad's internal standard |
| 11 | **Export signing key provenance** | The key is an operator-held 32-byte secret with a printed `key_id`; its authenticity rests on a written custody procedure, not on a signature from a trusted issuer. The signature is symmetric, so any verifier can also forge | AD-2: bind the key to an issued certification record, or replace HMAC with an asymmetric signature and a published public key |
| 12 | **Off-box replication** | **Partly closed 2026-11-10.** `backend/ledger_replication.py` now produces the D09 §4.5.4 series on a cadence — monthly full, weekly incremental, each bundle chained to the previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten — and its `inspect` verifies each bundle against the one before it and flags a missing period. What it does **not** do is move anything off the box, deliberately: D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no outbound network, so carrying the series away is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3. Until that step happens a lost disk still loses the ledger, and a missed run is *visible* in the series rather than prevented by it | Scheduled export to a second host, with the receipt acknowledged per D09 §4.4 |

Items 1 and 5 are **blocking** — the certification and detection claims cannot be made until they close. **Item 5's endpoint authentication closed 2026-11-11,** leaving the real payload schema as its only open part. **Item 1's entry half closed 2026-11-11:** a disposition now requires a live session token, and the reviewer identity on the row comes from that session rather than from the request. What keeps the item open is not the software's behaviour but the human process behind a credential — key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — which no amount of code settles; that process is now **written** (D09 §8.4) and is therefore auditable under §10.1, but writing it does not put a named person at the keyboard. The signed key directory is now built, and the item's last column records what it does and does not prove. Authenticating a credential holder is not authenticating a person, and this document does not claim it is. Items 3, 4, 6, 7, 11 and 12 are required before a production licence, not before a demo. Items 2, 8 and 9 are built. Item 10 is specific to the demonstration host and does not arise where the Platform runs on the Railroad's isolated network.

**Items 2 and 8, closed and what that changes.** The append-only guarantee is enforced by the database rather than by convention, and the export is signed and independently verifiable. Two suites test the two halves adversarially: 17 tests attempt an `UPDATE`, a `DELETE`, a second disposition, a tampered row and a removed row against the ledger, and 43 tests attempt to truncate, erase, extend, re-sign, reorder, re-key, wholly rewrite a bundle, and smuggle an unsigned field into one. A third suite of 58 tests attacks the attribution path: an attestation lifted onto another row, an attestation made under an unregistered, revoked, mismatched-reviewer or mismatched-certificate key, a registration date shifted, a registry entry edited or replaced, a manifest that miscounts what it carries, and a parity check that both verifiers catch the same seven structural tampers after the bundle is re-signed. **That suite was then handed to a separate agent whose instruction was to falsify the claim rather than review the code**, and it found a defect the whole suite had missed: the `reviewer` label in an exported attestation was not covered by the HMAC at all, so a holder of any registered reviewer key could relabel another reviewer's row and both verifiers returned a pass. It is fixed — the verifier must now be told which reviewer a key belongs to — and the reason it existed is §4.5a. **The erasure tests exist because the first version of this export passed a total wipe** — every row deleted, an honest empty bundle, a clean verification — and only an independent audit caught it. What remains open has moved from *"there is no signature"* to *"the signature cannot name the export signer, cannot date itself, and cannot detect a first-export-after-wipe"* — item 11, item 12 and the custody procedure. **Per-disposition attribution no longer belongs on that list**: a bundle can now say which registered reviewer attested a row.

## 8. Costs of the architectural choices

Stated plainly, because the Railroad's IT team will find them anyway and it is better that we said it first.

# The Master % Tracker, and the rubric that produces it

**Chat-11, 2026-11-13.** Rung 1 of the ladder.

---

## Why this file exists

The Master % Tracker has been reported at every phase open and close since
chat-9, as the owner instructed. Three of its four buckets have never had a
written rubric. The gap-row bucket was carried at **16.7** through chat-9's close
and chat-10's open and close without anything on disk that reproduces the number,
which means it could not be checked and would not be noticed if it drifted.

This file fixes that. It states the basis, scores every row against it, and
shows the arithmetic, so the next chat can **re-derive** the figure instead of
quoting a number out of a handoff.

## A correction to chat-11's own opening message

At the open of chat-11 I reported **16.4** for the gap-row bucket and **78.8**
total. I had not derived either — I adjusted chat-10's 16.7 by an impression and
wrote it down. Scoring the rows properly gives **16.0** and a total of **78.4**.

The error is small and the total barely moves, which is exactly why it needed
saying: the habit that produces a two-tenths error by impression is the same
habit that produced a 29x ROI error and a nine-defect audit in earlier chats.
**Derive, then write. If a number is in the message before it is in a table, the
order was wrong.**

---

## Basis — unchanged

| Bucket | Weight | What it counts |
|---|---|---|
| Docket documents | 40 | 37 docket IDs in D00 Part IV |
| B01 §7 gap rows | 30 | the 12 rows of B01 §7 |
| Core software | 20 | 8 named components |
| Release readiness | 10 | 5 named gates |
| **Total** | **100** | |

---

## Bucket 1 — Docket documents, 40.0 / 40

D00 Part IV is the authority. Read on 2026-11-13: **37 ID rows, all 37 carrying a
Built status** (34 as `**Built**`, B02 and B03 as `Built (.md)` / `Built (.html)`
with a format qualifier, A2 among the bold set). 37/37 → **40.0**.

This bucket cannot move. It measures documents existing, not documents being
correct.

## Bucket 2 — B01 §7 gap rows, 16.0 / 30

**The rubric.** Each of the 12 rows is scored 0–10 against one question: *how
much of the "Required for production" column exists?* The scale:

- **10** — the required state exists in the repository and is tested
- **7–9** — exists and is tested, with a named residual limit
- **4–6** — substantially built, the remaining part is blocked outside the repo
- **1–3** — the demo state is honest but the production state is untouched
- **0** — nothing

Each row carries `30 / 12 = 2.5` points at full score.

| # | Row | Score | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reviewer authentication | 6 | Session-gated entry, attestation at entry, signed key directory, custody procedure written. Held below 7 because "a credential holder is not a person" is a limit code cannot lift, and the signature is symmetric |
| 2 | Ledger append-only | 10 | Insert-only, triggers abort update/delete, SHA-256 chain, `INSERT OR REPLACE` refused. Built and attacked |
| 3 | Timestamps | 3 | Still SQLite `datetime('now')`; NTP is a host-level production step |
| 4 | Storage durability | 2 | Demo storage still ephemeral; persistent volume is Railroad hardware |
| 5 | Sensor ingest | 6 | Three gates, collector auth, fail-closed. Held below 7 because the payload schema is a demonstration one and nothing downstream scores an accepted payload |
| 6 | Time source | 2 | Host clock, unsynchronised |
| 7 | Update mechanism | 5 | `sign_release.py` builds a reproducible signed archive and verifies it; no GPG key, no custody, requirements unpinned, so the Docker build fails by design |
| 8 | Audit export | 9 | Signed, independently verifiable, chained, truncation- and rewrite-detecting, 48 adversarial tests. Held off 10 by the trust-anchor item |
| 9 | Repo hygiene | 10 | `.gitignore` present, `axiom.db` and `__pycache__` not tracked |
| 10 | TLS on the box | 2 | Plain HTTP on the demo host |
| 11 | Export signing key provenance | 3 | Symmetric; any verifier can forge; names no signer |
| 12 | Off-box replication | 6 | The cadence is built and `inspect` verifies it; carriage is the Railroad's physical step and nothing has moved |

**Sum 64 / 120 = 53.3% → 16.0 points.**

Cross-check on the shape rather than the digits: rows 2, 8 and 9 are the built
ones and score 29 of the 64; the six rows scoring 3 or below are all host-level,
organisational or blocked-externally. That distribution is the same story the
repo tells everywhere else, which is weak evidence the scoring is at least not
invented.

## Bucket 3 — Core software, 20.0 / 20

The eight components, named so the count is checkable rather than asserted:
physics engine (`physics.py`), ROI model (`roi.py`), fleet simulation
(`simulate.py`), warrant/advisory flow (`warrants.py`), disposition API and
frontend (`main.py` + `frontend/`), append-only ledger (`store.py`),
account/session auth (`accounts.py`), attribution registry
(`attribution.py`). All eight exist and are tested. 8/8 → **20.0**.

**A caveat worth writing down:** this bucket is generous. Five further modules
(`ingest.py`, `ingest_auth.py`, `ledger_export.py`, `ledger_replication.py`,
`key_directory.py`) also exist and are not counted, because the eight were fixed
in an earlier chat and silently re-basing the denominator upward would look like
progress. If a future chat wants them counted, that is a re-base and must be
disclosed as one, the way chat-10 disclosed its own.

## Bucket 4 — Release readiness, 2.4 / 10

The five gates, likewise named: SBOM generated, dependency downloads
hash-pinned, releases GPG-signed, transport secured (TLS or network isolation),
deployed on Railroad hardware. **None of the five is applied.** The 2.4 is
credit for the tools existing behind two of them (SBOM 15 tests,
`sign_release` 10) — 12% of the bucket, or about 0.6 of 5 gates.

That is deliberately stingy. Chat-9 scored "tool built, not applied" more highly
and chat-10 re-based down and disclosed it. This keeps chat-10's reading.

---

## The matrix

| Bucket | Weight | Open | Close | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Docket documents (37) | 40 | 40.0 | 40.0 | — |
| B01 §7 gap rows (12) | 30 | 16.0 | 16.0 | — |
| Core software (8) | 20 | 20.0 | 20.0 | — |
| Release readiness (5) | 10 | 2.4 | 2.4 | — |
| **Total** | **100** | **78.4** | **78.4** | **—** |

Against chat-10's close of 79.1, this is **−0.7 with nothing built in between**.
The movement is entirely my scoring of the gap rows: chat-10 carried 16.7
without a rubric, I re-derived 16.0 with one, and then corrected my own opening
figure of 16.4 to match. **A number that moves when nothing is built is a number
that was never derived.**

---

## What a future chat must do with this file

Do not quote 78.4. Re-score the 12 gap rows against the rubric above, at the
phase's open, and report what you get. If it differs from 78.4 and nothing was
built, the difference is the disagreement, and it is worth more than the number.

## Bucket 1 — Docket documents, 40.0 / 40

D00 Part IV is the authority. Read on 2026-11-13: **37 ID rows, all 37 carrying a
Built status** (34 as `**Built**`, B02 and B03 as `Built (.md)` / `Built (.html)`
with a format qualifier, A2 among the bold set). 37/37 → **40.0**.

This bucket cannot move. It measures documents existing, not documents being
correct.

## Bucket 2 — B01 §7 gap rows, 16.0 / 30

**The rubric.** Each of the 12 rows is scored 0–10 against one question: *how
much of the "Required for production" column exists?* The scale:

- **10** — the required state exists in the repository and is tested
- **7–9** — exists and is tested, with a named residual limit
- **4–6** — substantially built, the remaining part is blocked outside the repo
- **1–3** — the demo state is honest but the production state is untouched
- **0** — nothing

Each row carries `30 / 12 = 2.5` points at full score.

| # | Row | Score | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reviewer authentication | 6 | Session-gated entry, attestation at entry, signed key directory, custody procedure written. Held below 7 because "a credential holder is not a person" is a limit code cannot lift, and the signature is symmetric |
| 2 | Ledger append-only | 10 | Insert-only, triggers abort update/delete, SHA-256 chain, `INSERT OR REPLACE` refused. Built and attacked |
| 3 | Timestamps | 3 | Still SQLite `datetime('now')`; NTP is a host-level production step |
| 4 | Storage durability | 2 | Demo storage still ephemeral; persistent volume is Railroad hardware |
| 5 | Sensor ingest | 6 | Three gates, collector auth, fail-closed. Held below 7 because the payload schema is a demonstration one and nothing downstream scores an accepted payload |
| 6 | Time source | 2 | Host clock, unsynchronised |
| 7 | Update mechanism | 5 | `sign_release.py` builds a reproducible signed archive and verifies it; no GPG key, no custody, requirements unpinned, so the Docker build fails by design |
| 8 | Audit export | 9 | Signed, independently verifiable, chained, truncation- and rewrite-detecting, 48 adversarial tests. Held off 10 by the trust-anchor item |
| 9 | Repo hygiene | 10 | `.gitignore` present, `axiom.db` and `__pycache__` not tracked |
| 10 | TLS on the box | 2 | Plain HTTP on the demo host |
| 11 | Export signing key provenance | 3 | Symmetric; any verifier can forge; names no signer |
| 12 | Off-box replication | 6 | The cadence is built and `inspect` verifies it; carriage is the Railroad's physical step and nothing has moved |

**Sum 64 / 120 = 53.3% → 16.0 points.**

Cross-check on the shape rather than the digits: rows 2, 8 and 9 are the built
ones and score 29 of the 64; the six rows scoring 3 or below are all host-level,
organisational or blocked-externally. That distribution is the same story the
repo tells everywhere else, which is weak evidence the scoring is at least not
invented.

## Bucket 3 — Core software, 20.0 / 20

The eight components, named so the count is checkable rather than asserted:
physics engine (`physics.py`), ROI model (`roi.py`), fleet simulation
(`simulate.py`), warrant/advisory flow (`warrants.py`), disposition API and
frontend (`main.py` + `frontend/`), append-only ledger (`store.py`),
account/session auth (`accounts.py`), attribution registry
(`attribution.py`). All eight exist and are tested. 8/8 → **20.0**.

**A caveat worth writing down:** this bucket is generous. Five further modules
(`ingest.py`, `ingest_auth.py`, `ledger_export.py`, `ledger_replication.py`,
`key_directory.py`) also exist and are not counted, because the eight were fixed
in an earlier chat and silently re-basing the denominator upward would look like
progress. If a future chat wants them counted, that is a re-base and must be
disclosed as one, the way chat-10 disclosed its own.

## Bucket 4 — Release readiness, 2.4 / 10

The five gates, likewise named: SBOM generated, dependency downloads
hash-pinned, releases GPG-signed, transport secured (TLS or network isolation),
deployed on Railroad hardware. **None of the five is applied.** The 2.4 is
credit for the tools existing behind two of them (SBOM 15 tests,
`sign_release` 10) — 12% of the bucket, or about 0.6 of 5 gates.

That is deliberately stingy. Chat-9 scored "tool built, not applied" more highly
and chat-10 re-based down and disclosed it. This keeps chat-10's reading.

The movement is entirely my scoring of the gap rows: chat-10 carried 16.7
without a rubric, I re-derived 16.0 with one, and then corrected my own opening
figure of 16.4 to match. **A number that moves when nothing is built is a number
that was never derived.**

Do not quote 78.4. Re-score the 12 gap rows against the rubric above, at the
phase's open, and report what you get. If it differs from 78.4 and nothing was
built, the difference is the disagreement, and it is worth more than the number.

## 5. External network references

**None at runtime.** The application makes no outbound network connection of any kind — verified by inspecting every module for `urllib.request`, `http.client`, `socket`, and requests-style calls. The only `http://` strings in the codebase are **source citations in docstrings** for ROI figures (NTSB, DOJ, AP reporting), which are documentation and are never resolved.

The frontend references **no external URLs**. No CDN, no Google Fonts, no analytics beacon. A browser loading the dashboard contacts nothing but the local box.

> **This is the single most important statement in this document for the Railroad's security review.** It means the platform is compatible with a genuinely air-gapped network, not merely "deployable on-premise." See B05 for the full data-residency analysis.

## 6. Container and privilege posture

- Base image: `python:3.11-slim` — minimal Debian, no compiler or build tooling in the final image.
- **Runs as a non-root user** (`axiom`), created at build time, `/bin/false` shell.
- Container never requires root, never needs privileged mode, and mounts no host paths.
- Healthcheck uses only stdlib `urllib` against localhost.
- No OS-level packages installed beyond the base image and numpy.

## 7. Build and supply chain

| Concern | Current state |
|---|---|
| Dependency pinning | `numpy>=1.26` — **a floor, not a lock**. Production should pin exactly and vendor the wheel. |
| Hash verification | Not currently performed. Production should use `--require-hashes`. |
| SBOM | **Not produced.** A CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM should accompany every release (see D06). |
| Signed artifacts | Not currently signed. Required for offline updates (D06, C01). |
| Reproducible build | Not verified. |

**These four gaps are real and I am naming them rather than leaving them to be discovered.** None blocks a demonstration. All four block a production deployment into a Class I railroad, because their security review will ask for the SBOM and the signing chain and "we'll get to it" is not an answer.

## 8. Open-source licence obligations

BSD-3-Clause (numpy) and PSF-2.0 (Python) impose **no copyleft obligations**. There is no requirement to publish our source, no licence-compatibility conflict with commercial licensing, and no attribution burden beyond preserving the licence text in distributions — which should be included in every shipped artifact as a NOTICE file.

**Nothing in this stack prevents AxiomDynamics from licensing the platform commercially while keeping its source proprietary.** That matters for D07 (IP ownership) and for the escrow arrangement contemplated in D00 §III.11.

---

=== Dockerfile ===
# AxiomDynamics demo -- minimal image, on purpose.
# No OS-level build tools, no compiler, nothing beyond Python + numpy,
# consistent with the "immutable container on an air-gapped edge box"
# deployment story: this image has almost nothing in it to exploit.

FROM python:3.11-slim

LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="axiomdynamics-demo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.description="Physics-first predictive maintenance demo (thermo/kinematics/acoustics)"

# Run as a non-root user -- the container never needs root.
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/false axiom
WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
# --require-hashes is the half of hash pinning that enforces it. The pins live
# in requirements.txt, generated by tools/pin_requirements.py on a host with
# index access. Without this flag pip treats the hashes as comments and installs
# whatever the index serves under the pinned version, which is exactly the
# substitution the pins exist to stop.
#
# NOTE: requirements.txt is still a RANGE today, so this build fails until the
# release host runs `python3 -I tools/pin_requirements.py --write` and commits
# the result. That is deliberate. An unpinned dependency set should stop a
# release; it should not ship quietly with a flag that reads as a control and is
# not applied. See D09 §4.4, D10 Part 5.
RUN python -m pip install --no-cache-dir --require-hashes -r requirements.txt

COPY backend/ backend/
COPY frontend/ frontend/

RUN chown -R axiom:axiom /app
USER axiom

ENV AXIOM_PORT=8420
ENV AXIOM_HOST=0.0.0.0
EXPOSE 8420

# Basic liveness check -- hits the fleet endpoint, no extra deps needed.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=5s \
=== outbound check ===

Generate and verify a Software Bill of Materials for a Platform installation.

D09 §4.4 disclosed "no SBOM artefact in releases" as a supply-chain gap with a
Q1 2027 target. This closes it, and the way it closes it matters:

**The SBOM is generated from an installation, not from `requirements.txt`.**
A manifest that lists what we asked pip for is a shopping list; a manifest that
lists what pip resolved, unpacked and left on disk is an inventory. The gap D09
disclosed is that a Railroad cannot independently verify the dependency chain —
and a shopping list cannot be verified against anything, because it says nothing
about what actually arrived.

**The format is CycloneDX 1.5 JSON**, written directly rather than with a
library, for the same reason `tools/verify_ledger_export.py` imports nothing
from the Platform: a recipient must be able to read the artefact with a text
editor and a JSON parser. `cyclonedx-py` is a dependency, and adding a dependency
to generate the document about our dependencies is a joke that writes itself.
=== sign_release ===
"""
Build, sign and verify a release artefact (D09 §7.3, §4.4 target Q2 2027).

D09 §7.3 says, in bold, that Supplier does not sign release artefacts. This
changes that from a statement about us to a statement about a tool, and the
distinction the section already draws is the one this module keeps: **a release
signature and a ledger-export signature are different things.**

  * The ledger export signs DATA produced on the Railroad's host, with a
    symmetric key, so any verifier can also forge. §4.5a.
  * A release signs a BUILD we ship, with an asymmetric key, so a verifier can
    check authorship without being able to produce it. That is the whole reason
    to use GPG here rather than the HMAC the export uses: the export's threat is
    a Railroad insider changing a disposition; the release's threat is anybody

control that fails at exactly the moment it is needed.

content.text:
Byte-exact find/replace that preserves whatever line endings a file already uses.

Every docket edit in this project has to survive one trap: the working tree mixes
CRLF and LF, and a naive text round-trip rewrites every ending in the file. That
turned a one-line fix into a 167-line diff in chat-9 and a 1,248-line one in
chat-3. Read the bytes, replace in bytes, write the bytes back, and the endings
are whatever they were.

Usage:
    python3 -I tools/eol_edit.py <file> <old-file> <new-file>
    python3 -I tools/eol_edit.py <file> --show-ending

Old and new text are read from their own files so the caller never has to worry
about shell quoting. Newlines in those files are matched against EITHER ending in
the target, because the caller writes plain lines and cannot know which the
target holds.

Exit codes: 0 changed, 1 no match (nothing written), 2 matched more than once
(nothing written -- an ambiguous edit is refused, not guessed).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Tests for tools/eol_edit.py.

The whole reason this tool exists is that a text round-trip rewrote endings and
turned small edits into enormous diffs. So every test here asserts on the BYTES
of the result, not on what a text read would report -- a text read normalises the
very thing under test and would pass whether or not the file was damaged.
"""
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

TOOL = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "tools", "eol_edit.py")


def run(*args):
    proc = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "-I", TOOL, *args],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )
    return proc.returncode, proc.stdout, proc.stderr


class Sandbox:
    """A temp dir with helper writers, so each test states its own bytes."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()

def test_edit_hashing_a_docket_sized_file_is_single_line_diff():

    assert got == expected
    assert got.count(b"\r\n") == 200, got.count(b"\r\n")


class _report:
    def __init__(self):
        self.passed = 0
        self.failed = 0


def main():
    r = _report()
    for name, fn in sorted(globals().items()):
        if name.startswith("test_") and callable(fn):
            try:

            except AssertionError as exc:
                r.failed += 1
                print(f"FAIL  {name}: {exc}")
            except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001

                print(f"ERROR {name}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""B04's component inventory must match the code it claims to describe.

B04 opens by stating that every figure in it was checked against the code. The
inventory table then went four chats without changing while seven backend
modules were added, so it described 2,695 lines of a codebase that had grown to
8,200 -- and the seven it omitted were the cryptographic and authentication
modules a security reviewer spends their time on.

Correcting the table once does not fix that, because the same drift resumes the
moment the next module is written. So the table is now tested: every file it
names must exist with the line count it quotes, nothing in backend/ or
frontend/ may be missing from it, and the quoted total must equal the sum.

Deliberately NOT tested: that the numbers are "right" in some absolute sense.
The test's job is to make the document and the repository disagree loudly, and
it derives both sides from disk rather than from a list written here.
"""
import os
import re
import sys

ROOT = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), ".."))
DOCKET = os.path.join(ROOT, "client-assets", "MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET")
B04 = os.path.join(DOCKET, "B04-TECHNOLOGY-STACK-DISCLOSURE.md")

# A table row naming a source file and its line count:
#   | Dashboard logic | `frontend/app.js` | 595 | Vanilla JavaScript |
ROW = re.compile(r"^\|\s*[^|]+\|\s*`([a-z]+/[A-Za-z0-9_]+\.(?:py|js|css|html))`\s*\|\s*([0-9,]+)\s*\|", re.M)


def read(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        return fh.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")


def counted():
    """{relative path: physical line count} for every file the table may name."""
    out = {}
    for sub in ("backend", "frontend"):
        d = os.path.join(ROOT, sub)
        for name in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
            if not name.endswith((".py", ".js", ".css", ".html")):
                continue
            path = os.path.join(d, name)
            if not os.path.isfile(path):
                continue
            with open(path, "rb") as fh:
                out[f"{sub}/{name}"] = fh.read().count(b"\n")
    return out


def table_rows():
    return {m.group(1): int(m.group(2).replace(",", ""))
            for m in ROW.finditer(read(B04))}


def test_every_named_file_exists_with_the_stated_line_count():
    rows, actual = table_rows(), counted()
    assert rows, "the inventory table parsed as empty -- the format changed"
    wrong = []
    for path, quoted in sorted(rows.items()):
        if path not in actual:
            wrong.append(f"{path}: named in B04, not on disk")
        elif actual[path] != quoted:
            wrong.append(f"{path}: B04 says {quoted}, disk has {actual[path]}")
    assert not wrong, "B04 inventory is stale:\n  " + "\n  ".join(wrong)


def test_no_module_is_missing_from_the_inventory():
    """The defect that prompted this test: modules added, table not updated."""
    rows, actual = table_rows(), counted()
    missing = sorted(set(actual) - set(rows))
    # __init__.py is empty and carries no component; every other file is named.
    missing = [m for m in missing if not m.endswith("__init__.py")]
    assert not missing, "B04 omits code that exists: " + ", ".join(missing)


def test_the_quoted_total_equals_the_sum_of_the_rows():
    rows = table_rows()
    text = read(B04)
    m = re.search(r"^\|\s*\*\*Total\*\*\s*\|\s*\|\s*\*\*([0-9,]+)\*\*\s*\|", text, re.M)
    assert m, "the Total row is missing or changed format"
    quoted = int(m.group(1).replace(",", ""))
    assert quoted == sum(rows.values()), (
        f"total says {quoted}, rows sum to {sum(rows.values())}")


def test_the_supply_chain_section_does_not_claim_a_tool_is_absent():
    """A tool that exists is 'built, not applied' -- never 'not produced'.

    This is the second half of the same defect. B04 said 'Not produced' and
    'Not currently signed' while tools/sbom.py and tools/sign_release.py both
    existed and were tested.
    """
    text = read(B04)
    forbiddens = ["**Not produced.**", "Not currently signed",
                  "Not currently performed"]
    for phrase in forbiddens:
        assert phrase not in text, (
            f"B04 still says {phrase!r}, but the tool exists -- state it as "
            "'built, not applied'")


def test_every_supply_chain_row_names_its_three_state():
    """Each of the five controls must say built/not built/applied explicitly."""
    text = read(B04)
    section = text.split("## 7. Build and supply chain")[1].split("## 8.")[0]
    rows = [ln for ln in section.splitlines() if ln.startswith("| ") and "---" not in ln]
    # header + five controls
    assert len(rows) == 6, f"expected 6 table lines in section 7, found {len(rows)}"
    for ln in rows[1:]:
        assert ("**Tool built, not applied.**" in ln
                or "**Applied.**" in ln
                or "**Not built.**" in ln), f"row states no three-state status: {ln[:90]}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(0)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""B04's component inventory must match the code it claims to describe.

B04 opens by stating that every figure in it was checked against the code. The
inventory table then went four chats without changing while seven backend
modules were added, so it described 2,695 lines of a codebase that had grown to
8,200 -- and the seven it omitted were the cryptographic and authentication
modules a security reviewer spends their time on.

Correcting the table once does not fix that, because the same drift resumes the
moment the next module is written. So the table is now tested: every file it
names must exist with the line count it quotes, nothing in backend/ or
frontend/ may be missing from it, and the quoted total must equal the sum.

Deliberately NOT tested: that the numbers are "right" in some absolute sense.
The test's job is to make the document and the repository disagree loudly, and
it derives both sides from disk rather than from a list written here.
"""
import os
import re
import sys

ROOT = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), ".."))
DOCKET = os.path.join(ROOT, "client-assets", "MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET")
B04 = os.path.join(DOCKET, "B04-TECHNOLOGY-STACK-DISCLOSURE.md")

# A table row naming a source file and its line count:
#   | Dashboard logic | `frontend/app.js` | 595 | Vanilla JavaScript |
ROW = re.compile(r"^\|\s*[^|]+\|\s*`([a-z]+/[A-Za-z0-9_]+\.(?:py|js|css|html))`\s*\|\s*([0-9,]+)\s*\|", re.M)


def read(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        return fh.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")


def counted():
    """{relative path: physical line count} for every file the table may name."""
    out = {}
    for sub in ("backend", "frontend"):
        d = os.path.join(ROOT, sub)
        for name in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
            if not name.endswith((".py", ".js", ".css", ".html")):
                continue
            path = os.path.join(d, name)
            if not os.path.isfile(path):
                continue
            with open(path, "rb") as fh:
                out[f"{sub}/{name}"] = fh.read().count(b"\n")
    return out


def table_rows():
    return {m.group(1): int(m.group(2).replace(",", ""))
            for m in ROW.finditer(read(B04))}


def test_every_named_file_exists_with_the_stated_line_count():
    rows, actual = table_rows(), counted()
    assert rows, "the inventory table parsed as empty -- the format changed"
    wrong = []
    for path, quoted in sorted(rows.items()):
        if path not in actual:
            wrong.append(f"{path}: named in B04, not on disk")
        elif actual[path] != quoted:
            wrong.append(f"{path}: B04 says {quoted}, disk has {actual[path]}")
    assert not wrong, "B04 inventory is stale:\n  " + "\n  ".join(wrong)


def test_no_module_is_missing_from_the_inventory():
    """The defect that prompted this test: modules added, table not updated."""
    rows, actual = table_rows(), counted()
    missing = sorted(set(actual) - set(rows))
    # __init__.py is empty and carries no component; every other file is named.
    missing = [m for m in missing if not m.endswith("__init__.py")]
    assert not missing, "B04 omits code that exists: " + ", ".join(missing)


def test_the_quoted_total_equals_the_sum_of_the_rows():
    rows = table_rows()
    text = read(B04)
    m = re.search(r"^\|\s*\*\*Total\*\*\s*\|\s*\|\s*\*\*([0-9,]+)\*\*\s*\|", text, re.M)
    assert m, "the Total row is missing or changed format"
    quoted = int(m.group(1).replace(",", ""))
    assert quoted == sum(rows.values()), (
        f"total says {quoted}, rows sum to {sum(rows.values())}")


def test_the_supply_chain_section_does_not_claim_a_tool_is_absent():
    """A tool that exists is 'built, not applied' -- never 'not produced'.

    This is the second half of the same defect. B04 said 'Not produced' and
    'Not currently signed' while tools/sbom.py and tools/sign_release.py both
    existed and were tested.
    """
    text = read(B04)
    forbiddens = ["**Not produced.**", "Not currently signed",
                  "Not currently performed"]
    for phrase in forbiddens:
        assert phrase not in text, (
            f"B04 still says {phrase!r}, but the tool exists -- state it as "
            "'built, not applied'")


def test_every_supply_chain_row_names_its_three_state():
    """Each of the five controls must say built/not built/applied explicitly."""
    text = read(B04)
    section = text.split("## 7. Build and supply chain")[1].split("## 8.")[0]
    rows = [ln for ln in section.splitlines() if ln.startswith("| ") and "---" not in ln]
    # header + five controls
    assert len(rows) == 6, f"expected 6 table lines in section 7, found {len(rows)}"
    for ln in rows[1:]:

                or "**Applied.**" in ln
                or "**Not built.**" in ln), f"row states no three-state status: {ln[:90]}"

# D10 — Subprocessor & Third-Party Component Register

**Docket position:** D10. The register of every third party that touches Railroad data or ships inside the Platform.

**Classification:** Client-facing. Provided to the Customer's security review and maintained per release.

> **Why this document exists:** D02 §11, D07 §3.4, D13 §8 and B04 §7 all incorporate it by reference. A contract that incorporates a register that does not exist is a dangling obligation — and the first security auditor who asks to see it will discover the gap. This closes it.

---

## Part 1 — Subprocessors: none

**AxiomDynamics uses no subprocessors to process Railroad Data.**

There is no cloud hosting, no analytics vendor, no outsourced data processing, no third-party support desk, and no managed service provider with access to any deployment.

This is not a policy choice that could change quietly — it is a consequence of the architecture. Under AD-1 (B01), the Platform is fully on-premise and makes zero outbound network connections (B05, verified against code). Data that never leaves the Customer's network has no path to a subprocessor.

**Current subprocessor count: zero.**

| Subprocessor | Purpose | Data accessed | Location | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | — | — | — | None |

### If a subprocessor is ever added

Per D09 §7.1:

1. **30 days' advance written notice** to affected Customers.
2. The subprocessor is bound by confidentiality and security obligations **no less stringent than D09**.
3. The Customer **may object** within 30 days.
4. If the objection is unresolved, the Customer **may terminate the affected order without penalty**.

**Any change to this register is a contract-level event, not an administrative update.** It triggers notice under D09 §7.1 and appears in the release notes.

---

## Part 2 — Third-party runtime components

**One Python distribution, and seven libraries inside it.** This part previously
said "the complete inventory … one component", which was wrong in a way that
mattered: the numpy binary wheel does not ship one library. It bundles OpenBLAS,
LAPACK, a GCC Fortran runtime (`libgfortran`), `libquadmath`, `lapack-lite`,
`dragon4` and `libdivide`. These execute inside the Platform's own process. A
register that stops at the package name tells a security reviewer that we ship
one thing when we ship eight, and the eight are what a dependency-substitution
attack would actually target.

| Component | Version | Licence | Purpose | Source | Shipped as |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **numpy** | per `requirements.txt` | **BSD-3-Clause** | Numerical array operations for the physics computations | PyPI | Python wheel (platform-specific) |

Bundled inside the numpy wheel, and therefore inside the artefact we hand over:

| Bundled library | Licence | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenBLAS** | BSD-3-Clause | The BLAS/LAPACK implementation numpy links against |
| **LAPACK** | BSD-3-Clause-Attribution | Linear-algebra routines, compiled into the OpenBLAS build |
| **GCC Fortran runtime** (`libgfortran`) | **GPL-3.0 with the GCC Runtime Library Exception** | Fortran runtime the compiled BLAS needs; the Exception is what permits distribution inside a proprietary product |
| **`libquadmath`** | **LGPL-2.1-or-later** | GCC quad-precision maths library, linked by `libgfortran` |
| **`lapack-lite`** | BSD-3-Clause | numpy's fallback linear-algebra path |
| **`dragon4`** | MIT | Float-to-string conversion |

content.text:
### 4.4 Known gaps and remediation roadmap

The following controls are **not yet implemented** but are on the remediation roadmap:

| Gap | Impact | Remediation | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Authentication is local, not cryptographically registered** | A malicious insider with database access could potentially forge a disposition record. | Bind reviewer keys to authenticated accounts under AD-2 (per B01 §7 item 1) — the registry is **partly built 2026-11-11**, and **entry has been gated since 2026-11-11**: a disposition requires a live session bound to a certified account, identity comes from the session and never the body, and a certificate revoked mid-session stops writing. What remains is that a credential holder is not a person, and entry requires a session **and** an attestation: since 2026-11-11 a disposition is refused unless the caller presents a registered reviewer key matching the session's reviewer and certificate, and the attestation is written with the row or not at all | Q2 2027 |
| **The ledger export signature cannot name the signer** | **Split 2026-11-11 — the disposition half is closed, the export half is not.** The export bundle has been signed (HMAC-SHA256) and independently verifiable since 2026-11-09, and detects altered, added, reordered and removed records, a ledger that has shrunk since a bundle you already hold, and rows deleted from the front of the ledger. **What changed on 2026-11-11: a disposition row can now be bound to a registered reviewer and the binding verified by a recipient.** `backend/attribution.py` holds an append-only, **hash-chained** certification registry — not signed: it is tamper-evident to a re-computing reader, which is a weaker property than authentication and is stated as such in the module docstring — with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`INSERT OR REPLACE` refused, and each attestation is an HMAC over the row's own `record_hash` under that reviewer's 32-byte key, travelling inside the exported record. A recipient holding the reviewer key **and the name bound to it** recomputes it; one without the key still checks that the attestation names the reviewer and certificate the row names, that the key was registered before the attestation, and that the row was not recorded after the key was revoked. **What this does not close:** the *export* signature is still symmetric and unnamed — attribution is per-disposition, not per-bundle — the claim is about a key holder, not a human being at a keyboard (binding a key to a person is credential issuance under §4.5), the scheme is HMAC so a holder of reviewer A's key can attest as A, and it cannot prove **when** anything happened because no external timestamping exists on an air-gapped box. A wipe before the *first* bundle you ever receive also remains undetectable. **The entry half closed on 2026-11-11; the attestation half did not.** `backend/accounts.py` binds a local account to a live certification record and gates disposition entry on a bearer token, so the reviewer name and certificate on a row come from the session and **not** from the request; a free-text name is refused. A certificate revoked mid-session stops writing immediately. **What remains:** entry requires a live *session*, not an *attestation* — a row without an attestation is still an honest state the manifest counts rather than an error — and key custody and joiner/mover/leaver are a written procedure, **now written in §8.4** and still a procedure rather than a code control. | Bind export keys to certified identities under AD-2; require attestation as well as a session at entry; **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure — written §8.4**; signed key directory; move to an asymmetric signature with a published public key when a vetted library is available | Q2 2027 |
| **No automatic off-box replication of the ledger** | **Partly closed 2026-11-10.** The §4.5.4 series is now produced on its cadence by `backend/ledger_replication.py` — monthly full, weekly incremental, each chained to the last, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten — and `inspect` verifies every bundle against its predecessor and reports a missing period. What remains open is the **carriage**: the series is written to a directory on the Platform host and nothing moves it further, deliberately, because §3.2 promises the Platform has no outbound network. Moving the series to backup media is the Railroad's step under §3.3, and until it is done a lost disk still loses the ledger. A party with write access to the database file can still drop the triggers and recompute the chain between exports; only a recipient who **keeps each bundle as it arrives** detects that, which is why the custody procedure remains a control and not an administrative detail. | Off-box carriage of the produced series, with receipt acknowledgement; see B01 §4.5a and §7 items 11–12 | Q2 2027 |
